newsitem.title: UK: SFO not in contempt of court in Sumitomo case.
newsitem.headline: SFO not in contempt of court in Sumitomo case.

text.p: Judges found on Thursday that the director and four colleagues from Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) were not in contempt of court over the way they handled a raid in the course of their inquiry into the Sumitomo Corp scandal.
The High Court Tipstaff, an official who makes arrests, waited near the fraud squad just in case the judges had found against them and sent them to jail.
But the two senior judges ruled that, although SFO director George Staple's staff had breached the spirit of court orders in a raid on an accountancy firm, they were not in contempt.
The five SFO officials, Staple, lawyers Andrew Jackson and Christopher Walker, accountant Anne Dilks and computer expert Michael Hainey could, in theory, have been sentenced to prison.
"It has gone as we expected," Staple said of the proceedings. The case followed raids by the SFO on December 6 last year on the premises of Kay Accountants Ltd.

The SFO was accused of breaching a court order issued late on the day of the raid, banning them from milking information from six computers seized under search warrants, and ordering these to be returned to Kay.
The orders banning the SFO from downloading the machines and ordering their return were obtained by Kay director Jeffrey Green.
Lord Justice Staughton said the court considered there had been breaches in "the spirit of the order", but these had not amounted to contempt.
Regarding Staple, Staughton added that whatever the situation the court would not have considered any breaches of the court order would have justified contempt proceedings against him.
The SFO, in liaison with investigators in Japan and the United States, is investigating the multi-billion dollar scandal that rocked world metal markets in June last year.
Japanese conglomerate Sumitomo fired its head copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging he was a rogue who admitted running up losses of $2.6 billion in unauthorised copper trading.

After Lord Justice Staughton and Justice Scott Baker cleared the SFO team on the contempt issue the court was told by SFO counsel Edwin Glasgow that further proceedings aimed at obtaining judicial review of the original court orders had been settled.

Glasgow said the SFO accepted that the wording of the search and seize orders granted by London magistrates, which led to the computer seizure, had been worded in a way which resulted in uncertainty about them.
